name: Architect Scenarios
desc: 60 random scenario questions drawn from a 100-question bank, spread across all six official scenarios and weighted to the exam's domain blueprint.

questions.q: Your support agent's loop runs lookup_order, then sends the next request with only a new user message holding the tool_result. The API rejects it because the tool_result has no matching tool_use. What did the loop get wrong?
options: It sent the tool_result in a user message, when results belong in the system prompt so the model reads them as data
It reused the tool_use_id from the request, when every tool_result needs a freshly generated id of its own
It never appended the assistant's response, so the tool_use block the result answers is missing from history
It sent the result as plain text, when the API expects all tool output serialised as a JSON string in the content
questions.explain: Each turn the assistant's full content, including its tool_use block, must be appended before the user message that carries the tool_result with the matching tool_use_id; drop it and the result refers to nothing. The fresh-id option is the near-miss: ids are what links the two blocks, but the tool_result must reuse the tool_use_id it answers, not invent one. Results go in a user message, not the system prompt, and plain-text content is accepted.

questions.q: To stop runaway loops, a developer caps the support agent at 3 iterations. Simple questions still work, but refund cases needing get_customer, lookup_order and process_refund now end with 'I'll look into it'. What is the better loop design?
options: Loop while stop_reason is tool_use and stop on end_turn, keeping only a generous ceiling as a runaway backstop
Raise the cap to 6 iterations, since the longest refund path needs three tool calls plus a closing confirmation
Stop when the reply text contains a closing phrase such as 'anything else?', since that means the case is done
Ask the model to print DONE when finished and loop until that token appears, ignoring stop_reason on each turn
questions.explain: The model signals whether it needs more tool calls through stop_reason: tool_use means run the tools and continue, end_turn means it is finished. A high ceiling can stay as a safety net, but it should never be the normal exit. Raising the cap to 6 is the near-miss: it fixes today's longest path but is still an arbitrary limit that the next case with one extra lookup will hit. Watching reply text for a closing phrase or a DONE token is the parse-natural-language anti-pattern.

questions.q: Policy says process_refund may run only for a verified customer, so you gate it in the tool handler. Audit logs then show a refund on order ORD-5521 issued after the agent verified a different customer in the same chat. What should the gate check?
options: That get_customer returned a verified identity at some point earlier in the session, before the refund call
That the verified customer's id matches the customer id that owns the order passed to process_refund
That the system prompt contains the verification rule, so the model is reminded of it on every refund
That the agent restated the customer's name in its last reply, proving the verified account was in focus
questions.explain: The gate has to tie verification to the order being refunded: the verified customer id must equal the order's owner. The session-level 'verified at some point' check is the near-miss. It is a real programmatic gate, but it is exactly what let a refund go through on another customer's order after a different person was verified. Prompt reminders and restated names are not enforcement.

questions.q: When the support agent calls escalate_to_human, the receiving staff see only the escalation payload, not the chat. They keep re-asking customers for order numbers and what was already tried. What should the escalation pass?
options: The complete raw transcript, so the human has every message and can find whatever details they need
A short reason code such as POLICY_GAP, so routing can send the case to the right human queue quickly
A structured summary of the customer, orders, issue, steps taken, escalation reason and what they want
The model's confidence score and a sentiment rating, so the human can judge how urgent the case will be
questions.explain: A handoff should give the human the case facts up front, in a structure they can act on without reading the chat. The raw transcript is the near-miss: everything is in there, but the human has to dig for it, which is the delay the team is complaining about. A reason code alone drops the case details, and confidence and sentiment scores don't say what was tried.

questions.q: Refunds over $500 must go to a human. The team adds a PostToolUse hook on process_refund that escalates when the amount is over 500, yet finance still sees large refunds paid out. Why, and what fixes it?
options: PostToolUse fires only for MCP tools; the refund tool must be re-registered as an SDK tool for the hook to intercept it
The hook needs a matcher naming process_refund; without one it runs on every tool and skips the amount check silently
PostToolUse fires after the refund has run; a PreToolUse hook must block calls over $500 and tell the agent to escalate
Hooks are only advisory; the $500 limit must also be written into the system prompt so the model chooses to respect it
questions.explain: PostToolUse runs after the tool has executed, so by then the money has moved. Blocking has to happen in PreToolUse, which can deny the call and return a reason the agent acts on by escalating. The missing-matcher option is the near-miss: matchers do scope which tools a hook sees, but no matcher can make a post-execution hook prevent the call. Hooks are deterministic, not advisory.

questions.q: get_customer returns the full card number and the security-question answer along with the profile. Compliance says the model must never see either value. Where should they be removed?
options: In the system prompt, telling the model never to repeat card numbers or security answers to anyone
In a PreToolUse hook that checks get_customer's arguments and blocks calls that ask for card data
In a final output filter that scans each reply to the customer and masks anything like a card number
In a PostToolUse hook that redacts both values from the tool result before it reaches the model
questions.explain: Removing the values from the tool result before the model reads it guarantees the model never sees them, deterministically. The output filter is the near-miss: it stops the values reaching the customer, but the model has already read them, which is what compliance forbids. A prompt rule only governs what the model repeats, and get_customer's arguments don't request card data, so there is nothing to block before the call.

questions.q: The support agent's design doc lists four requirements. Which TWO must be enforced in code (hooks or tool gates) rather than left to system-prompt instructions? (Select 2)
options: No refund over $500 is paid out unless a human approves it first
Replies stay friendly and avoid jargon when explaining policy
Identity is verified before any change is made to an account
The agent offers the satisfaction survey link before signing off
questions.explain: Requirements where a single miss causes financial or security harm need deterministic enforcement: the refund limit and the identity check before account changes. Tone and the survey link are style and process preferences where an occasional miss is harmless, so prompt guidance is enough. The survey link is the tempting pick because it is a hard 'always do this' rule, but missing it costs nothing that needs a guarantee.

questions.q: An architect proposes replacing the support agent's free tool selection with a hard-coded flowchart: classify the intent, then follow a fixed tool sequence per branch. Many cases mix billing, shipping and account problems. What is the better design?
options: Keep the flowchart but add an LLM classifier at every branch, so mixed cases can still move between the paths
Use the flowchart for every case, and call escalate_to_human whenever a case doesn't fit one branch cleanly
Let the model choose tools from what each result shows, with programmatic gates only before irreversible actions
Let the model choose tools with no gates at all, trusting detailed tool descriptions to keep refunds in policy
questions.explain: Model-driven selection adapts to cases that cross categories, and the risky steps still get deterministic gates. Adding an LLM classifier at every branch is the near-miss: it uses the model, but still forces cases through pre-configured paths and multiplies the number of classification points that can go wrong. Escalating everything that doesn't fit a branch wrecks first-contact resolution, and removing the gates drops the guarantees.

questions.q: process_refund's amount parameter expects integer cents, but its schema just says amount: number, 'the refund amount'. The agent sometimes passes 49.99 for a $49.99 refund, and the customer receives $0.50. What is the best fix?
options: Add a system-prompt line reminding the agent that all money values in tool calls should be in cents
Rename the parameter to amt, so the model treats it as an internal field and copies values unchanged
Accept both forms and guess the unit from whether the number has a decimal point, then convert it
Describe the parameter as integer cents with an example (4999 for $49.99), and type it as an integer
questions.explain: Input formats belong in the tool interface itself: the parameter description and type, with a worked example, are what the model reads at the moment it builds the call. The system-prompt reminder is the near-miss: it holds the right information, but away from the schema the model is filling in, and the schema still invites a decimal. Renaming the field obscures it further, and guessing the unit turns 50.00 into an ambiguity.

questions.q: process_refund fails when the payment gateway times out, and the tool returns the text 'Error: refund failed'. The agent then tells customers their refund cannot be processed. How should the tool report this failure?
options: Return isError: true with errorCategory 'business', isRetryable: false, so the agent stops and escalates instead
Retry inside the tool until the gateway responds, then return success, so the agent never sees a failure at all
Return isError: true with errorCategory 'transient', isRetryable: true and a note that the gateway timed out
Return a success result with status 'pending', so the agent reassures the customer while finance checks later
questions.explain: A timeout is a transient failure, and saying so in a structured way lets the agent retry or tell the customer it is temporary instead of refusing. The 'business' category is the near-miss: the structure is right, but labelling a timeout as a policy outcome makes the agent treat a temporary fault as a final no. Unbounded retries inside the tool hide the problem, and reporting 'pending' misstates what happened.

questions.q: During a database outage, lookup_order caught the connection error and returned an empty orders list. The agent told several customers they had no orders on file. What change to lookup_order prevents this?
options: Keep the empty list but add a message field reading 'no orders found or lookup failed' for the model to weigh
Return isError: true with an access-failure category when the query fails, and an empty list only on success
Put HTTP status 503 in the result text, which the model recognises as an outage and passes on to the customer
Raise an unhandled exception, so the whole agent run stops and the customer sees a generic service error page
questions.explain: An empty list has to mean 'the query worked and found nothing'. A failed query must come back as a structured error, so the agent never confuses the two. The combined message is the near-miss: it admits a failure is possible but leaves the model guessing which of two very different states it is in. A status code buried in the text is unstructured, and crashing the whole run is the opposite anti-pattern.

questions.q: Every support conversation must load the account with get_customer before anything else. In testing, the agent sometimes calls lookup_order first. How do you guarantee get_customer is the first call?
options: Set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} on the first request, so the model must call a tool before it replies
Keep tool_choice auto and list get_customer first in tools, since order in the request sets the priority
Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "get_customer"} on the first request, then go back to auto
Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "get_customer"} on every request in the conversation
questions.explain: Forcing the named tool on the first request guarantees the prerequisite call, and returning to auto lets the conversation continue normally. tool_choice any is the near-miss: it guarantees that some tool is called, but the model can still pick lookup_order. Forcing get_customer on every request would trap the agent calling it repeatedly, and tool order is not a priority setting.

questions.q: Part-way through a refund the agent is about to complete, the customer writes: 'I'd rather just talk to a person.' What should the agent do?
options: Honour the request and call escalate_to_human now, passing a summary of the case and the refund in progress
Finish the nearly complete refund first, then offer a human only if the customer repeats the request afterwards
Ask what is wrong with the help so far, so it can fix the problem and avoid an unnecessary handoff to a person
Check the customer's sentiment score first, and escalate only if the message reads as frustrated or upset
questions.explain: An explicit request for a human is a valid trigger to escalate, and the agent should act on it straight away, passing on the refund it was working on. Finishing the refund first is the near-miss: it looks efficient, but it overrides what the customer clearly asked for. Questioning the request or gating it on a sentiment score makes the same mistake.

questions.q: A patient customer has given three order numbers, and lookup_order finds none of them. Each time, the agent asks them to double-check and try again. What should the agent do now?
options: Keep asking for another order number, since the customer is calm and the next one may well match
Tell the customer that no orders exist under their details and close the case as resolved for now
Escalate to a human with a summary of the three failed lookups, since the case is making no progress
Check the customer's sentiment, and keep trying for as long as the messages stay polite and patient
questions.explain: Repeated attempts that make no progress are a valid reason to escalate, and the summary saves the human from repeating the failed lookups. Checking sentiment is the near-miss: the customer's patience feels like permission to keep going, but sentiment says nothing about whether the case can be solved. Asking again repeats the loop, and closing the case turns a lookup failure into a false answer.

questions.q: The team is writing rules for when the support agent hands off to a human. Which TWO are reliable escalation triggers? (Select 2)
options: The message scores below -0.6 on a sentiment classifier
The request falls in a situation no written policy covers
The model rates its own confidence below 70% on its answer
Several attempts to resolve the issue have made no progress
questions.explain: A gap in policy and repeated failure to make progress are both reliable signals that a human is needed. Sentiment is a poor proxy: an angry customer may have a simple fix, and a calm one may have a case that needs a human. Self-reported confidence is the near-miss: it sounds like a measure of when to hand off, but the model's self-ratings are not calibrated and don't track when it is actually wrong.

questions.q: lookup_order returns about 40 fields per order, including warehouse codes, carrier scan logs and internal SKUs. In long chats with several orders, the agent's context fills quickly and early details get missed. What helps most?
options: Summarise the conversation every ten turns, so the old order results are condensed into short paragraphs
Trim each lookup_order result to the fields the agent uses (status, items, amounts, dates) before it is added
Ask the agent to call lookup_order again whenever it needs an order, rather than relying on earlier results
Move the order results to the end of the context each turn, since recent content gets the most attention
questions.explain: Most of each result is fields the agent never uses, so trimming it to what matters, in the tool or a PostToolUse hook, stops the bloat at its source. Regular summarisation is the near-miss: it does shrink the context, but only after the noise has gone in, and summaries can blur exact amounts and dates. Re-calling the tool adds more of the same bloat, and moving results around doesn't make them any smaller.

questions.q: A developer says Claude Code ignores the team's rule to use pnpm rather than npm in this repo. What is the quickest way to see which memory files actually loaded in their session?
options: Run /config, which shows the settings in effect and the CLAUDE.md file each of those settings came from
Run /memory, which lists the CLAUDE.md and rule files loaded for the session and lets you open them
Run /init, which regenerates CLAUDE.md and reports which of the existing rules it found and then kept
Run /doctor, which checks the installation and lists any CLAUDE.md files that failed to load or parse
questions.explain: /memory shows which memory files are loaded and opens them for editing, which quickly shows whether the project CLAUDE.md, or the rule file holding the pnpm rule, is actually in play. /config is the near-miss because it is also a configuration view, but it covers settings, not memory files. /init writes a new CLAUDE.md rather than diagnosing the current one, and /doctor checks the installation.

questions.q: The project CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines covering API style, testing, deployment and security. It is hard to maintain, and reviewers can't tell what changed where. What is the recommended restructure?
options: Move each topic into a CLAUDE.md in the matching subdirectory, so each loads only in that part of the tree
Move it to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so it stops cluttering the repository and still loads for every developer
Turn every section into a skill, so none of it loads until a developer runs the matching slash command
Split it into topic files under .claude/rules/ or pull them in with @path imports, keeping CLAUDE.md short
questions.explain: Topic files in .claude/rules/, or @imports, keep each concern in its own reviewable file while still loading it as project memory. Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files are the near-miss: they do modularise, but they load only when Claude works in that directory, and topics like security and API style apply across the whole tree. User-level memory isn't shared through version control, and skills don't load standing conventions automatically.

questions.q: A team command in .claude/commands/new-migration.md takes a table name, but developers keep running it with no argument. Which frontmatter field shows the expected argument in the command picker?
options: argument-hint, which shows a placeholder such as <table-name> after the command as you type
description, which sets the summary shown beside the command name while the picker is open
allowed-tools, which lists the tools the command may use and prompts for any inputs they need
model, which picks the model for the command and asks for any missing input before it starts
questions.explain: argument-hint shows the expected arguments during autocomplete, so the command tells people it needs a table name. description is the near-miss: it is also shown in the picker, but it summarises what the command does rather than showing an argument placeholder. allowed-tools pre-approves tools and model picks the model; neither asks for input.

questions.q: A developer has a personal /standup command that summarises their own commits since yesterday. They want it in every repository they work in, without adding it to any team's repo. Where should it live?
options: In ~/.claude/commands/standup.md, a user-scoped command available in every project on their machine
In .claude/commands/standup.md inside each repository, committed so it is there whenever they clone
In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, as an instruction to summarise recent commits whenever they type 'standup'
In .claude/settings.json in each repository, registered under a commands key with the prompt inline
questions.explain: User-scoped commands in ~/.claude/commands/ follow the developer into every project without touching shared repos. Project commands are the near-miss: it is the same mechanism, but a committed copy in each repository adds a personal tool to every team's codebase, which is what they wanted to avoid. A CLAUDE.md instruction isn't a command, and settings.json doesn't define commands.

questions.q: The team has a 300-line release checklist covering version bumps, the changelog, tagging and smoke tests. It is needed only when someone cuts a release, about twice a month. Where should it live?
options: In the project CLAUDE.md, so every step is always in context and Claude never misses one when a release starts
In .claude/rules/release.md with paths: ["CHANGELOG.md"], so it loads only while the changelog is edited
In the release manager's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so only the one person who cuts releases ever has it loaded
In a skill under .claude/skills/release/, so the procedure loads on demand when a release is actually run
questions.explain: A skill is the right home for a long procedure used now and then: its content loads only when the task is run, and the whole team shares it. The path rule is the near-miss: it also loads on demand, but rules attach guidance to editing matching files, and a release starts well before the changelog is touched and covers many files. Putting it in CLAUDE.md costs context in every session, and user-level memory isn't shared.

questions.q: A rule file .claude/rules/testing.md has the frontmatter paths: ["src/**/*.test.ts"]. It loads when Claude edits src/user.test.ts but not when it edits packages/api/src/order.spec.ts. Why?
options: Rules load only from the directory nearest the edited file, so packages/api needs its own .claude/rules folder
Path rules are checked once per session, so after the first test file the rule is cached and not checked again
The glob matches only .test.ts files under the top-level src/, so .spec.ts files in packages/ never match it
The paths key accepts directory names only, so the value must be src/ rather than a glob with a file suffix
questions.explain: The rule loads only for files matching its glob, and src/**/*.test.ts matches neither the .spec.ts suffix nor anything under packages/. A pattern list such as ["**/*.test.ts", "**/*.spec.ts"] fixes it. The nearest-directory option is the near-miss: that is how subdirectory CLAUDE.md files behave, but path rules sit in the project's .claude/rules/ and are matched by glob. paths takes glob patterns, and rules aren't cached after the first match.

questions.q: Two pieces of guidance: 'every change needs a changelog entry', which applies to all work, and React component conventions for the .tsx files spread across five packages. Where should each one go?
options: Changelog rule in CLAUDE.md; component conventions in a .claude/rules/ file with paths: ["**/*.tsx"]
Both in .claude/rules/ files with paths: globs, so each loads only while Claude edits a matching file type
Changelog rule in CLAUDE.md; component conventions in a CLAUDE.md placed in each of the five packages
Both in the project CLAUDE.md, so every session loads them whatever files happen to be worked on
questions.explain: Guidance that applies to all work belongs in CLAUDE.md. Conventions for one file type spread across the tree are what glob-scoped rules are for: they load only when a .tsx file is edited. Five subdirectory CLAUDE.md files are the near-miss: they would work, but they duplicate one convention five times and miss any new package. Path-scoping the changelog rule would hide it whenever no matching file is touched.

questions.q: You need to rename a private helper, formatPrice, which is used only in cart.ts and its test file. Which approach fits?
options: Enter plan mode so Claude can map every caller and present a plan for your approval before it edits
Spawn an Explore subagent to survey the codebase for callers, then make the change when it reports
Record a naming decision in CLAUDE.md first, so the convention exists before Claude makes the change
Use direct execution: the change is small and well scoped, so ask for the rename and run the tests
questions.explain: A well-scoped change in two known files suits direct execution. Plan mode is the near-miss: it is the safe choice for large, multi-file or architectural work, but here its exploration and approval step cost more than the change itself. An Explore subagent is for verbose discovery, and nothing here needs discovering.

questions.q: In plan mode for a session-to-JWT auth migration, Claude reads about 200 files to find every touchpoint. By the time it drafts the plan, its early findings are getting muddled. What should change?
options: Hand discovery to an Explore subagent that reads the files and returns a concise map of the touchpoints
Run /compact after the discovery phase, so the file contents are summarised before the plan gets drafted
Switch to direct execution and migrate one module at a time, committing after each so nothing is lost
Raise the model's max output tokens, so the plan has room to cover every file read during the discovery
questions.explain: Verbose discovery is what the Explore subagent is for: the 200 file reads stay in its context, and the planning session gets a compact map. /compact is the near-miss: it does shrink the context, but only after the damage is done, and its summary may drop the very touchpoints the plan needs. Skipping planning for a cross-cutting auth change is risky, and output tokens are not the constraint.

questions.q: You have described three times, in prose, how parseDuration should handle inputs like '1h30m', '90s' and '2d', and Claude keeps getting edge cases wrong. What is the most effective next step?
options: Rewrite the prose description in more detail, spelling out each rule for units, ordering and leading zeros
Give concrete inputs with their exact expected outputs, edge cases included, or tests that encode them
Ask Claude to rate its confidence in each rule, then revisit only the rules where it reports low confidence
Switch to plan mode, so Claude writes a full design for the parser before it tries another implementation
questions.explain: When prose keeps being misread, concrete input/output examples or tests remove the ambiguity and give a pass/fail target. More detailed prose is the near-miss: it seems like the obvious next step, but the problem is that prose is ambiguous, and more of it adds more room for misreading. Self-rated confidence isn't reliable, and planning won't settle what the expected outputs are.

questions.q: A code review left five issues: three touch validateOrder and change how its errors are raised, caught and shown; two are typos in unrelated modules. How should you give them to Claude?
options: Send all five in one message, so Claude has the full list and can fix everything in one combined pass
Send each of the five issues one at a time, checking every fix before moving on to the next one in turn
Send the two typos first as warm-up fixes, then the three validateOrder issues one by one after that
Send the three validateOrder issues together in one message, and handle the two unrelated typos apart
questions.explain: Fixes that interact belong in one message, so Claude can make one consistent change to how errors are raised, caught and shown. Independent issues can be handled separately. One at a time is the near-miss: it is careful, but each validateOrder fix can undo or clash with the one before. Lumping all five together mixes unrelated work into the same change.

questions.q: You ask Claude Code to remove the deprecated v1 API from a large repo. Nobody knows how many callers exist or what patterns they use. Which decomposition fits best?
options: Run a fixed chain of steps set up front: update routes, then clients, then tests, then the documentation
Discover the callers first, generate subtasks from what turns up, and add new ones as more patterns appear
Ask for the whole removal in one pass, then run the test suite at the end to catch anything that was missed
Split the repository alphabetically into four parts and run the same removal prompt on each part in turn
questions.explain: When the shape of the work is unknown, subtasks should come from what discovery finds and adapt as new caller patterns turn up. The fixed chain is the near-miss: its steps sound complete, but they were decided before anyone knew what the callers look like, so unusual usages fall between stages. One big pass and an arbitrary alphabetical split both ignore the structure of the work.

questions.q: A nightly script runs claude -p to continue the same code-generation conversation each night. Other scripts on that build machine also run claude in the same directory. How should it resume the right session?
options: Pass --continue on the next run, which picks up the most recent session in the working directory
Save the final assistant reply and send it as the opening prompt of a fresh session on the next night
Save the session id from the run's JSON output and pass it with --resume on the next night's run
Keep the process alive between runs, so the session stays in memory and needs no resume step at all
questions.explain: Resuming by session id targets exactly the conversation this job started. --continue is the near-miss: it does resume, but it takes the most recent session in the directory, which on a machine shared with other scripts may be someone else's. Replaying the final reply loses the tool history, and keeping a process alive overnight isn't a resumption design.

questions.q: You ask Claude Code to add i18n to 120 React components in one pass. It drifts: later files use different key naming from earlier ones. How should the task be split up?
options: Split the components into two halves and run each half in a parallel session to finish the job more quickly
Run per-file passes against a written key convention, then a separate cross-file pass that checks consistency
Repeat the single pass three times, since each repetition corrects more of the drift left by the one before
Convert all 120 files, then have Claude self-review its own changes in the same session before it finishes
questions.explain: Per-file passes keep each unit of work small, and a dedicated cross-file pass catches inconsistencies that no single-file pass can see. Two parallel sessions is the near-miss: it does split the work, but it creates two independent naming conventions instead of one. Repeating the same pass doesn't fix how the task is split, and self-review in the same session tends to confirm its own choices.

questions.q: While fixing a flaky test, Claude runs the full suite each iteration and the 3,000-line output lands in context every time. After a few rounds it loses track of which failures it has fixed. What helps most?
options: Run /clear after each iteration, so every test run starts from an empty context and nothing gets confused
Move test results to the middle of the prompt, where the model gives long logs more balanced attention
Ask Claude to summarise the full output after each run, adding each summary to the end of the session
Trim the test output to the failing tests and their errors before it reaches context, key results first
questions.explain: Verbose tool output crowds out the facts that matter. Trimming it to failures, with key results first, keeps the context lean and readable. A summary after each run is the near-miss: it shortens things, but the full 3,000 lines still land in context first, and the summaries pile up. /clear throws away the record of what was already fixed, and the middle of a long context is where detail is most easily lost.

questions.q: Midway through a run, one search subagent fails. In the research system's hub-and-spoke design, which component decides whether to retry it, reroute the work or report the gap?
options: The coordinator, since every subagent's results and errors flow back to it and it owns the overall plan
The synthesis subagent, since it is the next consumer of the search results and knows what it is missing
The failed search subagent, which restarts itself and notifies the other subagents of its new results
The report subagent, since it writes the final output and can tell the reader which sections are thin
questions.explain: In hub-and-spoke, every subagent reports back to the coordinator, which holds the plan and so decides how to handle each failure. The synthesis subagent is the near-miss: it does feel the gap first, but it has no view of the plan and no authority to dispatch work, and subagents don't call one another. The failed subagent can retry transient errors locally, but it can't reroute work or notify its peers.

questions.q: The analysis subagent keeps drifting into writing polished final-report prose instead of returning structured findings. Its AgentDefinition prompt says only 'You are a helpful research assistant.' What is the fix?
options: Add the role limits to the coordinator's system prompt, so it reminds itself what analysis should return
Remove the report subagent, since analysis is already producing prose that is good enough for readers
Give the analysis subagent more tools, so it has other work to do and spends less effort on writing up
Give its AgentDefinition a role-limiting prompt: analyse only, return the findings schema, write no prose
questions.explain: A subagent's behaviour is set by its own system prompt, the prompt field of its AgentDefinition, so a role-limiting prompt there keeps it to analysis and its output format. The coordinator's system prompt is the near-miss: the instructions are right, but the subagent never sees the coordinator's prompt because its context is isolated. Removing the report stage, or adding tools, ignores the misconfigured role.

questions.q: The coordinator splits a question into four independent subtopics and spawns a search subagent for each, one per turn, waiting for each to finish. Runs take four times longer than they need to. What should change?
options: Give a single search subagent all four subtopics, so it covers them inside one long-running context
Have each search subagent spawn the next one when it finishes, chaining them without the coordinator
Lower each subagent's max_tokens, so every search returns sooner and the sequential total comes down
Emit all four Task calls in a single coordinator response, so the four searches run in parallel
questions.explain: Several tool calls in one response run in parallel, so independent subtasks should be spawned together. One subagent covering all four is the near-miss: it removes the turn-by-turn waiting, but the subtopics are still worked through one after another, in one context that fills up. Chaining bypasses the coordinator and stays sequential, and shorter outputs only cut a little time from each sequential step.

questions.q: The coordinator delegates with: 'Analyse the documents about grid-scale battery costs.' The analysis subagent returns generic text with none of the figures from the sources the search agent found. What is the fix?
options: Give the analysis subagent WebSearch, so it can find the documents itself rather than depending on others
Tell the analysis subagent in its system prompt to recall what the search subagent found earlier on
Run the analysis subagent with a larger context window, so it can hold the coordinator's earlier history
Put the search findings, the extracted figures and each source's URL and date directly in the Task prompt
questions.explain: Subagents start with isolated context: they see only what the coordinator puts in the Task prompt, so findings and source metadata must be passed explicitly. Giving it WebSearch is the near-miss: the subagent would get documents, but it repeats the search and may pick different sources from the ones the run already chose. It can't recall what it never saw, and a bigger window doesn't import the coordinator's history.

questions.q: Reports often miss angles that only come to light after the first round of research, such as a regulation mentioned in a single source. How should the coordinator handle this?
options: Run more search subagents in the first round, so the initial sweep is wide enough to catch every possible angle
Check the synthesis against the question, find gaps and send targeted follow-up searches before reporting
Ask the report subagent to list the missing angles in a 'further reading' section at the end of the report
Give the synthesis subagent WebSearch, so it can fill in any gaps it notices while merging the findings
questions.explain: An iterative refinement loop lets the coordinator judge coverage after each round and send focused work at the gaps it finds. A wider first sweep is the near-miss: it raises cost on every run, yet still can't search for an angle nobody knows about until a source mentions it. Listing gaps as further reading leaves them unresearched, and giving synthesis a search tool blurs its role.

questions.q: Two search subagents, one asked about 'EV battery supply chains' and one about 'lithium sourcing', return mostly the same sources, wasting calls. What is the best fix?
options: Deduplicate sources in the synthesis step, so the overlap is removed before the findings reach the report
Have the coordinator partition the scope explicitly, giving each subagent distinct subtopics and exclusions
Run the two subagents one after the other, so the second can see and skip whatever sources the first found
Merge the two into a single subagent covering both topics, so it can avoid repeating any source on its own
questions.explain: The overlap comes from how the coordinator split the work, so the fix is clearer partitioning: distinct scopes and explicit exclusions in each prompt. Deduplicating at synthesis is the near-miss: the report comes out clean, but the duplicate searches have already been paid for. Running them in sequence gives up parallelism, and merging them throws away the benefit of the split.

questions.q: The coordinator sends every query to all four subagents (search, analysis, synthesis and report), even a one-line factual check such as a company's founding year. What is the better design?
options: Have the coordinator decide per query which subagents it needs, and skip those that add nothing to it
Keep all four for every query, since a fixed path makes the system's behaviour easier to predict
Add a fifth classifier subagent that labels each query and then still runs all four stages after it
Let each subagent decide for itself whether to run, by checking the query against its own description
questions.explain: The coordinator should pick subagents dynamically from what each query needs, so a simple check doesn't pay for four stages. The classifier subagent is the near-miss: it adds the right kind of judgement, but then ignores it by still running every stage. A fixed path wastes cost and time, and subagents don't receive queries on their own to decide about.

questions.q: When the coordinator spawns the analysis subagent with the Task tool, what does the new subagent have in its context?
options: Its own definition's prompt and the Task prompt, but not the coordinator's history or system prompt
The coordinator's system prompt and tools, but none of the conversation turns that came before the call
The coordinator's full conversation so far, so it can see the findings and decisions already made
Everything every other subagent has produced in this run, since subagents share one research workspace
questions.explain: Subagents run in isolated contexts. They start from their own definition and the Task prompt (plus shared project setup such as CLAUDE.md), not from the coordinator's conversation, which is why everything they need must be written into that prompt. Inheriting the coordinator's system prompt is the near-miss: it sounds like a sensible partial share, but the subagent runs under its own definition's prompt, not the coordinator's. Neither the conversation history nor other subagents' output is passed on automatically.

questions.q: The coordinator gives the analysis subagent a 14-step procedure: open each PDF, find table 2, extract column C, and so on. It fails whenever a source is laid out differently. What delegation style should replace it?
options: A more detailed procedure that adds a branch for each layout seen so far, so the steps cover every format
A shorter procedure with only the first five steps, leaving the subagent to improvise anything after that
A goal-oriented brief: the objective, the constraints, the output schema and the quality bar for the result
A one-line goal with no constraints or schema, so the subagent has full freedom over what it sends back
questions.explain: Goal-oriented delegation states what to achieve and what good output looks like, and lets the subagent adapt its steps to each source. The one-line goal is the near-miss: it is goal-oriented, but with no constraints or output schema the results won't fit what synthesis needs. Adding more branches only covers layouts already seen, and cutting the procedure short is still procedural.

questions.q: Searches on separate subtopics are independent, synthesis needs all of their results, and the report needs the synthesis. Which orchestration pattern fits this research run?
options: Fully sequential: run every search, then synthesis, then the report, one subagent at a time from start to end
Fully parallel: start searches, synthesis and the report together, each refining its output as data arrives
Peer-to-peer: let each search subagent message the synthesis subagent directly as soon as it finds results
Parallel fan-out for the searches, then synthesis once all return, then the report: parallel, then sequential
questions.explain: Independent work should run in parallel, and steps that depend on earlier results must wait for them, so the searches fan out and synthesis and the report follow in order. Fully sequential is the near-miss: the order is correct, but it serialises searches that don't depend on each other. Fully parallel starts synthesis before its inputs exist, and peer-to-peer messaging bypasses the coordinator.

questions.q: The report subagent was given WebSearch 'in case it needs it'. Reports now include claims from sources the search phase never vetted, with no citations. What is the best fix?
options: Remove WebSearch and give the report subagent only the tools its role needs, with a role-limiting prompt
Keep WebSearch, but tell the report subagent in its prompt to cite every new source it finds while writing
Add a citation-checker subagent after the report, so any uncited claims get flagged before the report ships
Set the report subagent's tool_choice to auto, so it calls WebSearch only when it judges a search necessary
questions.explain: Each subagent should hold only the tools its role needs. A report writer with a search tool will go and find new material, which is how unvetted claims got in. The citation checker is the near-miss: it catches some of the damage later, but leaves the cause in place and adds a stage. Asking it to cite new sources still lets unvetted sources in, and auto is already the default.

questions.q: A search subagent hits a 429 rate-limit on one of its six queries. Today the coordinator receives the raw error and restarts the whole subagent. What is the better pattern?
options: Have the subagent skip the failed query quietly and return its other five results as if the search were complete
Return the failure to the coordinator at once with isRetryable: false, so it can pick another subagent to use
Retry the query in the subagent with backoff, and pass up a structured error only if it keeps failing
Have the coordinator lower its overall request rate, then rerun every subagent from scratch after a pause
questions.explain: Transient errors should be recovered where they happen. The subagent retries with backoff and escalates, with structured context, only what it can't fix. Passing the failure straight up is the near-miss: escalating with structure is right for unrecoverable errors, but a 429 is retryable by nature, and marking it not retryable misleads the coordinator. Skipping the query silently hides a gap, and rerunning everything wastes the five queries that succeeded.

questions.q: A research run crashed after three of its five search subagents had finished. Restarting re-ran all five and doubled the cost. How should the pipeline be designed so it can resume?
options: Keep all subagent outputs in the coordinator's context, so a restart can read them back from its history
Use the fork_session option on restart, so the new run inherits the results from the run that crashed
Run all five searches inside one agent, so there is a single unit of work to restart if anything fails
Save each subagent's output with a state manifest of completed tasks, and skip completed ones on restart
questions.explain: Writing results and a manifest of what is done to durable storage lets a restart skip completed work. The fork_session option is the near-miss: forking does branch from an existing session's history, but it isn't a checkpoint of completed pipeline tasks, and it doesn't tell the restarted run which subagents to skip. In-memory context doesn't help after a crash, and one big unit makes every restart cost the full run.

questions.q: One of five search subagents fails permanently because its source site blocks automated access. The other four return good results. What should the coordinator do?
options: Carry on with the four results and say in the report which subtopic is missing and why it couldn't be covered
Abort the whole run, since a report built on four of five subtopics is incomplete and could mislead readers
Drop the failed subtopic quietly and build the report from the four that worked, so the output stays clean
Retry the failed subagent in a loop until the site lets it through, holding the report until all five succeed
questions.explain: A partial result with the gap clearly stated is more useful than nothing, and more honest than a silent omission. Aborting is the near-miss: it sounds rigorous, but ending the whole workflow over one blocked source is an anti-pattern just as silent suppression is. Dropping the subtopic quietly hides the gap, and a permanent block won't clear however many times you retry.

questions.q: A report presents a finding backed by one preprint with the same certainty as a finding backed by six peer-reviewed studies that agree. Readers can't tell which conclusions are settled. What should change?
options: Add a general disclaimer at the top of the report noting that some findings rest on less evidence than others
Drop every claim backed by fewer than three sources, so the report contains only well-established findings
List all sources in a bibliography sorted by publication type, so readers can judge the evidence themselves
Have synthesis record evidence strength per claim (source count, type, agreement) and word claims to match
questions.explain: Synthesis should keep the difference between well-established and contested or thinly supported findings, carrying evidence strength with each claim so the report's wording can reflect it. The disclaimer is the near-miss: it admits the evidence varies but doesn't say which claims it applies to. Dropping thin claims throws away possibly important early evidence, and a sorted bibliography leaves readers to rebuild the claim-to-source links themselves.

questions.q: Two credible sources disagree: one reports 34% adoption among hospitals in 2024, the other 41%. Both are relevant to the report. How should synthesis handle this?
options: Report both figures with their sources, and note the conflict and any known cause such as methodology
Report the figure from the more authoritative source in the text, and note the other figure in a footnote
Report the average of the two figures, 37.5%, citing both, so the reader gets a single central estimate
Leave the statistic out altogether, since contested figures weaken the report and invite misquotation
questions.explain: Synthesis should keep uncertainty at the source level: give both figures with attribution and flag the disagreement, so readers can see it is contested. The footnote option is the near-miss: it keeps both numbers, but it still picks a winner and downgrades credible evidence to a footnote. Averaging produces a figure neither source reported, and leaving it out hides relevant evidence.

questions.q: You are defining the search subagent's output schema so that synthesis can keep provenance. Which TWO fields matter most? (Select 2)
options: A source URL or document id attached to each extracted claim
A single overall confidence score for the whole search result
A word count of the text the subagent read during each search
The publication date and publisher recorded for every source
questions.explain: Claim-level source ids let synthesis trace each fact to where it came from, and date and publisher let it weigh and explain conflicting figures. A single overall confidence score is the near-miss: it sounds like it captures reliability, but it flattens per-claim uncertainty into one number and links nothing to a source. A word count says nothing about provenance.

questions.q: An engineer asks the agent to list every SQL migration file whose name matches *_add_*_column.sql anywhere in the repository. Which built-in tool fits best?
options: Grep, searching file contents for add_ and column across every SQL file in the repository
Read, opening the migrations folder and scanning its listing for names matching the pattern
Glob, matching **/*_add_*_column.sql against file paths without opening any of the files
Bash, running cat on every .sql file and filtering the combined output for add_column lines
questions.explain: Glob matches file paths by pattern, which is exactly a name-based search. Grep is the near-miss: it is the right tool for searching inside files, but this request is about file names, and matching on content would also catch files that merely mention adding a column. Read opens one file at a time, not a recursive listing, and cat-ing every file floods the context.

questions.q: To change one line in a 2,000-line config module, the agent uses Write to rewrite the whole file. Now and then other lines come back slightly altered or missing. What should it do instead?
options: Use Edit with an old_string that matches the target line uniquely, so only that part of the file changes
Read the whole file first, then Write it back with the change applied, so it has the exact text in hand
Use Bash with a heredoc to rewrite the file, which streams it to disk more reliably than the Write tool
Split the module into smaller files first, so each Write call regenerates less text and makes fewer slips
questions.explain: Edit changes only the matched text, so the rest of the file can't drift. That is the right tool for a targeted change. Read then Write is the near-miss: it is the documented fallback when no unique anchor exists, but it still regenerates all 2,000 lines, which is where the slips come from. A heredoc has the same problem, and splitting the module is a large change made only to work around the wrong tool.

questions.q: An engineer asks which command the repository's dev script runs. The script is defined in package.json at the repository root. Which tool should the agent use?
options: Grep for the word dev across the repository, collecting every file that mentions it before deciding
Glob for **/package.json, then open every match in turn to find whichever one defines a dev script
Read on package.json, since the file's path is already known and the answer sits in its scripts block
Bash running npm run dev, so the agent can watch the output and work out what the script really does
questions.explain: When the exact file is known, Read it directly. Glob for every package.json is the near-miss: Glob is the right tool when you don't know where files are, but here the path is given, and in a monorepo it would pull in packages nobody asked about. Grepping for 'dev' returns noise, and running the script has side effects and still doesn't show its definition.

questions.q: A developer wants their personal notes MCP server available in every project they open, but never shared with teammates. They run claude mcp add notes … with no scope flag, and it works only in the current repo. What should they do?
options: Re-add it with --scope project, so it is written to .mcp.json, then keep that file out of version control
Keep the default scope and run the same add command once in each project they want the server in
Re-add it with --scope user, so it is stored in their user config and loads in all of their projects
Add it to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, so Claude knows the server exists and loads it in every project they open
questions.explain: User scope makes a server available across all of a person's projects without putting it in any repository. The default is local scope, which is private but tied to the current project, as they saw. Repeating the default add in every project is the near-miss: the scope is right for privacy, but it means manual setup per project that drifts over time. Project scope is for sharing, and CLAUDE.md doesn't configure servers.

questions.q: Mid-session, a developer adds a new docs server to the project's .mcp.json. Claude can't see any of its tools, although the servers configured before the session work fine. What explains this?
options: A server's tools appear only after its first successful call, so Claude must try a docs tool by name once
MCP servers are discovered when the session connects, so the new one appears after the session restarts
Only one project-scope server can be active at a time, so the new entry is ignored until the old one goes
A new server's tools must also be named in CLAUDE.md, since Claude calls only MCP tools that memory lists
questions.explain: Configured servers are discovered when the session connects, so a server added mid-session isn't connected until the session is restarted. The first-call option is the near-miss: it treats the tools as lazily loaded on use, but Claude can't call a tool from a server it never connected to. Many project servers can be active at once, and CLAUDE.md doesn't control which tools are available.

questions.q: A code Q&A subagent that only needs to answer questions about the codebase was given Write, Edit and Bash along with Read, Grep and Glob. While answering, it sometimes 'helpfully' fixes code. What is the best fix?
options: Keep all six tools, and add 'do not modify files' to the subagent's prompt as a firm instruction
Limit the subagent to Read, Grep and Glob, the tools its question-answering role actually requires
Keep all six tools, but set tool_choice to auto so it uses Write only when it judges an edit needed
Add a PostToolUse hook that reverts any file the subagent writes, so edits never survive the run
questions.explain: Each subagent should hold only its role's tools. A read-only role with no write tools can't modify code, which also shrinks its tool choices. The revert hook is the near-miss: it undoes the damage, but the subagent still makes edits that a hook then has to clean up, and anything it ran through Bash may not be revertible. A prompt rule is a request, not a limit, and auto is already the default.

questions.q: The productivity agent has one tool, repo_action(action, params), whose action accepts nine values such as 'search', 'blame' and 'open_pr'. The agent often passes the wrong params for an action. What is the best fix?
options: Add a long list of every action and its params to the system prompt, so the agent can look it up as needed
Split it into separate tools, each with its own description, input schema and examples for its one action
Make every param optional, so the tool accepts any combination and ignores fields an action doesn't use
Keep the single tool but rename the action values to longer names that hint at the params each one needs
questions.explain: A generic tool hides nine different interfaces behind one schema. Separate tools give each operation its own description and a precise input schema the model can follow. The system-prompt reference is the near-miss: it supplies the missing information, but in a place far from the tool schema, which still accepts any params for any action. Making params optional hides the errors, and renaming the values doesn't define their inputs.

questions.q: Engineers keep asking the agent to scaffold a REST endpoint (handler, test and route entry) in the team's exact style. How should this be packaged for the whole team?
options: A personal command in ~/.claude/commands/new-endpoint.md that each engineer copies to their machine
A paragraph in CLAUDE.md describing the endpoint steps, so they are loaded into every session by default
A project command in .claude/commands/new-endpoint.md that takes the endpoint name as $ARGUMENTS
A PostToolUse hook that adds the test and route entry each time Claude writes a new handler file to disk
questions.explain: A project-scoped command lives in the repo, so everyone gets it with the code, and $ARGUMENTS passes in the endpoint name. The personal command is the near-miss: it is the same mechanism in the wrong scope, so each copy drifts and new hires don't have it. A CLAUDE.md paragraph adds to every session's context and isn't invoked on demand, and a hook can't generate code in the team's style.

questions.q: Before letting the agent refactor a legacy pricing module that has no tests, which workflow gives the most reliable result?
options: Have it refactor the whole module in one pass, then ask it to review the diff carefully for behaviour changes
Have it explain the module in detail first, then refactor based on its explanation of what the code should do
Have it refactor in plan mode, since planning first guarantees the refactor keeps the existing behaviour
Have it write characterisation tests that pin current behaviour, then refactor and iterate until they pass
questions.explain: Tests that pin current behaviour turn 'don't change behaviour' into a check that can be run, and the agent can iterate against it. Explaining the module first is the near-miss: understanding helps, but the explanation is unverified and gives no pass/fail signal when the refactor drifts. Reviewing its own diff tends to confirm its own work, and planning doesn't guarantee behaviour stays the same.

questions.q: The team lists four requirements for the agent. Which TWO need a settings permission rule or a hook rather than an instruction in CLAUDE.md? (Select 2)
options: Prefer small, focused functions over long multi-purpose ones
Claude must never read files matching .env or secrets/**
Every Bash command must be checked against a blocklist first
Explain the reasoning behind any non-obvious design decision
questions.explain: Rules that must hold without exception need mechanisms that enforce them: a permission deny rule for reading secret files, and a PreToolUse hook to check Bash commands. Function size and explaining design decisions are judgement-based guidance, which suits CLAUDE.md. The function-size rule is the tempting pick because it reads like a firm standard, but an occasional exception is acceptable, so it doesn't need enforcing.

questions.q: An engineer wants to understand how three legacy services (billing, inventory and shipping) talk to each other. Exploring all three in the main session would flood its context. What is the best approach?
options: Spawn three exploration subagents in parallel, one per service, each returning a short interface summary
Explore all three in the main session, then run /compact once, so only a summary of the findings is retained
Spawn one subagent that explores all three services in turn and returns its full notes on every file it read
Ask the engineer to explore each service in three separate sessions and paste their conclusions back in
questions.explain: Parallel subagents keep each service's verbose exploration in its own context and hand back concise summaries for the main session to connect. One subagent with full notes is the near-miss: it does isolate the exploration, but returning every note pushes the bulk straight back into the main context, and the services are explored one after another. Compacting after the fact loses detail, and the agent can do this work itself.

questions.q: Your developer agent's custom loop runs only the first tool_use block in each response. When the model asks for three Read calls at once, the next request fails because two tool_use blocks have no result. How should the loop be fixed while keeping parallel tool calls?
options: Run every tool_use block in the response and return all the tool_results together in the next user message
Run every tool_use block, but send each tool_result back as a separate user message, one request apiece
Disable parallel tool use, so the model asks for one file per turn and the loop never sees two blocks
Run only the first block and drop the rest, telling the model in a note that one call per turn is allowed
questions.explain: Every tool_use block in a response needs a matching tool_result, and they all go back together in one user message, which is also what makes parallel tool calls pay off. Separate messages is the near-miss: every call gets run, but splitting the results across requests leaves the first request with unanswered tool_use blocks and breaks the turn structure. Disabling parallel calls breaks the stated requirement to keep them, and dropping blocks recreates the error.

questions.q: A multi-hour codebase investigation keeps hitting context limits, and after each /compact the agent repeats searches it has already done. What practice prevents the lost work?
options: Disable automatic compaction, so the session keeps every earlier tool result until the investigation is complete
Have the agent keep a scratchpad file of findings and open questions, and re-read it after each compaction
Run /compact more often, so each summary is smaller and keeps a larger share of the findings already made
Ask the agent to restate all its findings in every reply, so the latest summary is always near the context end
questions.explain: A scratchpad file keeps findings outside the context window, so they survive compaction and can be re-read when needed. Compacting more often is the near-miss: it keeps the session under its limit, but each summary can still drop the details that stop repeat searches. Turning compaction off just means hitting the hard limit, and restating everything each turn fills the context faster.

questions.q: In a codebase investigation, most of the main session's context is now raw Grep and Read output from dozens of searches, and answer quality is dropping. What change addresses the cause?
options: Delegate searching to subagents that return distilled findings, keeping raw output out of the main session
Run /compact every few searches, so the raw output is summarised before it builds up in the main context
Switch to a model with a larger context window, so all the raw search output fits without crowding anything
Ask the agent to answer from memory where it can, so it runs fewer searches and adds less output overall
questions.explain: The cause is raw search output landing in the main context. Subagents do the searching in their own contexts and return only the findings. Frequent /compact is the near-miss: it keeps the context smaller, but it is a lossy cleanup after the raw output has already come in, and repeated summaries lose detail. A bigger window postpones the problem, and answering from memory trades accuracy for space.

questions.q: A CI step runs claude -p with --output-format json, but the review findings inside the result change shape from run to run, breaking the parser. Which flag makes the output follow a fixed structure?
options: --output-format stream-json, which emits one strictly typed event per finding instead of one combined result
--json-schema, passing a JSON Schema that the structured result must validate against before it returns
--verbose, which adds the full turn-by-turn messages to the output so the parser can find the findings
--append-system-prompt, adding 'always answer in the same JSON shape' to the prompt on every run of the job
questions.explain: --json-schema makes the run's structured output conform to a schema you supply, so the shape is guaranteed. --append-system-prompt is the near-miss: asking for a fixed shape usually works, but it is prompt-based formatting with no guarantee, which is exactly the variation the parser is hitting. stream-json streams events about the session, not a schema for your findings, and --verbose adds noise.

questions.q: A CI review job once looped for 50 minutes and ran up a large bill. Which TWO CLI options put a hard limit on a non-interactive run? (Select 2)
options: --verbose, which logs every turn so a runaway is spotted sooner
--continue, which resumes the last session instead of a new one
--max-turns, which caps the number of agentic turns in the run
--max-budget-usd, which stops the run at a set API spend limit
questions.explain: --max-turns caps how many agentic turns a print-mode run can take, and --max-budget-usd stops it once spending reaches a set amount. Together they stop runaway CI jobs. --verbose is the tempting pick because it helps you see a runaway, but logging doesn't stop anything. --continue changes which session runs, not how long it runs.

questions.q: On a shared self-hosted runner, claude -p review jobs pick up hooks, plugins and a user-level CLAUDE.md left by whoever set up the machine, so results vary and startup is slow. What gives a reproducible run?
options: Run with --bare, skipping auto-discovery of hooks, plugins and CLAUDE.md, and pass needed context explicitly
Run with --permission-mode plan, so hooks and plugins can't execute and the review stays strictly read-only
Delete ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md at the start of each job, which removes every local customisation the run loads
Run with --output-format json, which isolates the run from local settings and returns structured results
questions.explain: --bare starts a minimal session that skips auto-discovered hooks, plugins and CLAUDE.md, so what the job loads is exactly what it passes in through flags. Deleting the user CLAUDE.md is the near-miss: it removes one source of drift, but leaves the hooks, plugins and other local settings that are also loaded. Plan mode limits actions, not configuration discovery, and the output format has no effect on what loads.

questions.q: The CI review bot keeps flagging raw SQL in the reports/ directory, which the team allows there on purpose. Every claude -p run starts fresh. Where should this accepted pattern be recorded?
options: In a comment on each pull request, so the reviewer sees the exception in the PR thread before it reviews
In the first review's session, then resume that session in every later job so the exception carries forward
In the project CLAUDE.md, or a rule file it loads, so every CI run picks up the standards and the exception
In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on a developer laptop, since that is where the team lead keeps review preferences
questions.explain: Project memory is loaded on every run, so standards and accepted exceptions placed there reach every fresh CI review. Resuming one session is the near-miss: it does carry context forward, but it ties every job to one aging session and its history instead of versioned configuration. Per-PR comments have to be repeated on every PR, and a laptop's user memory never reaches the runner.

questions.q: A CI job runs claude -p to generate tests. It must create and edit test files and run npm test, nothing else. Runs keep stalling or failing on permission checks. What is the right configuration?
options: Pass --dangerously-skip-permissions, so the job never stops on a permission check during generation
Pass --allowedTools with Read, Edit, Write and Bash(npm test:*), pre-approving only what the job needs
Pass --permission-mode plan, so Claude proposes the tests and the runner applies them in a later step
Pass --verbose, so the permission prompts are written to the log where the runner can answer them
questions.explain: Pre-approving exactly the tools the job needs lets it run without prompts while still refusing anything else. Skipping all permissions is the near-miss: the stalls go away, but so does every guardrail, so the job could run any command. Plan mode stops edits altogether, and a CI log can't answer a prompt.

questions.q: The CI review job needs extra instructions that local sessions must not get: comment only on changed lines and end with a JSON summary. Shared review standards already live in CLAUDE.md. Where should the CI-only instructions go?
options: In the project CLAUDE.md under a 'CI only' heading, so the job and local sessions read the same file
In the CI invocation, via --append-system-prompt, keeping CLAUDE.md for the standards everyone shares
In a .claude/rules/ file with paths: [".github/**"], so it loads only when CI workflow files are edited
In ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on the CI runner's image, which the job loads in addition to the project file
questions.explain: Instructions that belong only to the CI run go on that run's command line. --append-system-prompt adds them without changing what local sessions load. The 'CI only' heading is the near-miss: the job would read it, but so would every local session, and a heading doesn't stop the model applying it. A path rule triggers on editing workflow files, not on running in CI, and image-level user memory is configuration hidden from the repo.

questions.q: The review prompt says 'be conservative and only report important issues', yet developers get a dozen naming and style comments per PR. What change cuts this noise most reliably?
options: Repeat 'be conservative' more forcefully, adding that minor issues waste the team's time and erode trust
Define categories to report (bugs, security, data loss) and to skip (style, naming), with code examples
Ask the model to rate each finding's importance from 1 to 10 and report only findings that score above 7
Shorten the prompt so the model has less to weigh, letting it focus on whatever matters most in the diff
questions.explain: Explicit categories with examples replace a vague instruction with a boundary the model can apply consistently. The 1 to 10 importance score is the near-miss: it looks like a precise filter, but the score rests on the same undefined idea of 'important', so the noise just moves into the ratings. Repeating 'be conservative' louder and shortening the prompt leave the criteria undefined.

questions.q: Developers have started ignoring the review bot: about 40% of its comments are false positives, mostly 'possible null dereference' and 'inefficient loop'. What should you do first?
options: Add a confidence threshold, posting only findings the model rates above 80% across every category it checks
Keep every category but add a note to each comment saying it may be a false positive the reader can ignore
Disable those two categories until their criteria are rewritten, keeping the high-precision categories live
Add more categories, so the share of real issues rises and the false positives become a smaller fraction
questions.explain: False positives erode trust in every comment, including the true ones, so the noisy categories come off first and go back only once their criteria are precise. The confidence threshold is the near-miss: it seems to target the problem, but self-rated confidence isn't calibrated, and it filters every category rather than fixing the two that are failing. Disclaimers make the bot easier to ignore, and new categories don't remove any false positives.

questions.q: A rule says 'flag network calls without error handling'. The bot now flags every fetch in test files and calls already wrapped by the team's withRetry helper. How should the criterion be revised?
options: Add explicit exclusions: skip test files and calls wrapped in withRetry, with an example of each kind
Soften it to 'flag network calls that might lack error handling', so the bot applies more judgement
Drop the rule, since error handling is a style preference best left to each developer's discretion
Keep the rule and add a post-filter that drops every finding whose text mentions the word 'fetch'
questions.explain: Good criteria state exclusion boundaries as well as inclusions, with examples, so known accepted patterns stop being flagged. Softening the wording is the near-miss: it sounds like it would reduce over-flagging, but 'might lack' is vaguer than before and invites more judgement calls, not fewer. Dropping the rule loses real findings, and a keyword filter throws out true positives along with false ones.

questions.q: On 30-file PRs, a single review pass gives detailed feedback on the first files, thin feedback on later ones, and misses an API contract broken across two files. What review structure fits?
options: One pass over all files with a larger max_tokens, so the review has room to cover each file in full depth
Two identical full passes over the whole PR, merging the findings so the second catches what the first missed
One pass per file for local issues, then a separate cross-file pass that looks at interfaces and data flow
One pass per file only, since issues confined to single files make up most of the bugs a reviewer finds
questions.explain: Per-file passes give every file the same attention, and a dedicated cross-file pass catches problems, such as a broken contract, that only show when files are read together. Per-file only is the near-miss: it fixes the uneven depth but by design can't see the issue that spans two files. More output room doesn't fix attention spread across 30 files, and repeating an identical pass repeats its blind spots.

questions.q: The review bot now attaches a self-reported confidence to each finding, and the team wants to use it to cut false positives. Which use is sound?
options: Route findings by confidence after checking on labelled PRs how well each level predicts a real bug
Post only findings above a fixed confidence such as 0.8, since the model knows best how sure it really is
Drop the confidence field entirely, since a self-reported confidence carries no signal about quality
Have the model raise its own threshold over time, reporting higher confidence as its accuracy improves
questions.explain: Self-reported confidence is only useful once it is calibrated against known outcomes. Measured that way, it can sensibly route findings. The fixed 0.8 cut-off is the near-miss: it uses the signal, but uncalibrated self-ratings often don't track accuracy, so a fixed gate may hide real bugs and keep confident false positives. Throwing the field away wastes a usable signal, and a model can't recalibrate itself.

questions.q: The review bot's first pass finds real bugs but also plausible-looking false ones. You want to filter the findings before they are posted. Which second step works best?
options: Ask the same conversation 'are you sure about each finding?' and keep the ones it still stands behind
Run the same review prompt a second time and post only the findings that appear in both of the runs
Ask the first pass to append a confidence score and post only the findings it rates as very likely
Send each finding with its code to a separate instance that must confirm or reject it on the evidence
questions.explain: An independent instance that sees only the finding and the code judges it fresh, which is what catches plausible false positives. Asking 'are you sure?' in the same conversation is the near-miss: it is a second look, but the reviewer is anchored on its own earlier reasoning and tends to defend it. Re-running the same prompt repeats the same biases, and uncalibrated self-scores filter poorly.

questions.q: A nightly job sends 5,000 file reviews through the Message Batches API. Results come back in a different order from the requests. How do you match each result to its file?
options: By position: results always come back in the same order the requests were listed in the batch
By the custom_id you set on each request, which is returned on the matching result to join on
By the message id the API assigns to each request when the batch is first created and accepted
By the file path, which the model puts at the start of every response it writes in the batch
questions.explain: Each batch request carries a custom_id that comes back on its result, and that is how you join results to inputs, since order isn't guaranteed. Position is the near-miss: it seems natural for a list, but it is exactly what breaks when results arrive out of order. The API doesn't hand back per-request message ids at creation for you to match on, and relying on model output to identify the file is fragile.

questions.q: The team wants the nightly batch review to let Claude call a read_file tool to open related files as needed, within each batch request. Why won't that work, and what should they do instead?
options: Batch requests don't accept tool definitions at all, so the job has to move wholly to the synchronous API
A batch request can't run a multi-turn tool loop, so include the related files in each request up front
Batch requests run tools on Anthropic's side, so read_file must be uploaded as a hosted tool with the batch
Batch requests time out after one hour, too short for tool calls, so the requests must be split up smaller
questions.explain: Each batch request is a single model call: there is no chance to run a tool and send back the result within that request, so the files the model needs must be included up front. 'No tool definitions at all' is the near-miss: it names the right limitation area, but tools can be defined in batch requests; what's missing is the multi-turn loop. Batches can take up to 24 hours, and custom tools aren't hosted by Anthropic.

questions.q: Merged PRs must have a debt report within 36 hours of merging. Reports run through the Message Batches API, which can take up to 24 hours to process. What is the longest interval you can leave between batch submissions?
options: 6 hours, which leaves a wide safety margin on top of the 24 hours a batch can take to finish processing
24 hours, so each daily batch gathers one full day of merges and finishes its processing within a day
36 hours, since each batch then covers exactly the window the merged PRs are allowed for their report
12 hours, since a PR can wait that long for the next submission and then up to 24 hours for its result
