questions.explain: Worst case, a PR merges just after a submission, waits a full interval, then waits up to 24 hours for processing, so the interval plus 24 must be no more than 36, which makes it 12 hours. 6 hours is the near-miss: it also meets the deadline, but it isn't the longest interval, so it submits twice as often as needed. 24- and 36-hour intervals both allow worst cases beyond 36 hours.

questions.q: When a 60-file PR is reviewed in one call, the findings JSON is often cut off before it closes. Raising max_tokens helps for a while, until bigger PRs arrive. What is the durable fix?
options: Raise max_tokens to the model's maximum, so even the largest PRs fit inside a single call's output limit
Ask the model to keep each finding to one short sentence, so the full JSON fits within the current limit
Prefill the response with an opening brace, so the model starts the JSON at once and wastes no tokens
Split the review into smaller scoped calls, such as per file or per module, and merge the findings after
questions.explain: Output truncation on large inputs is fixed by splitting the work into scoped calls whose output fits, then merging, which scales with PR size. Raising max_tokens to the maximum is the near-miss: it buys headroom, but that limit is finite and the next larger PR truncates again. Terser findings lose information and only delay the problem, and a prefill saves a handful of tokens.

questions.q: payment_terms is an enum of net_30, net_60 and due_on_receipt. Contracts with wording like 'payable promptly' or 'terms as agreed' get forced into one of the three. What is the recommended schema pattern?
options: Add an 'unclear' value plus a payment_terms_text field that holds the original wording from the document
Keep the three values and tell the model to pick whichever is closest whenever the wording is ambiguous
Replace the enum with a free-text field, so every contract's wording is captured exactly as it is written
Make payment_terms required, so the model has to commit to one of the three values for every document
questions.explain: An 'unclear' value lets the model report ambiguity honestly, and keeping the source text lets a person or a later rule resolve it. Picking the closest value is the near-miss: the output stays tidy for downstream systems, but it turns ambiguous terms into confident wrong ones. Free text loses the structure downstream systems rely on, and forcing a choice causes exactly the problem described.

questions.q: document_type is an enum of invoice, receipt and credit_note. Pro-forma invoices and delivery notes keep being labelled 'invoice' and flowing into accounts payable. What is the best schema change?
options: Remove the enum and accept any free-text string, so the model can describe each document in its own words
Add a confidence field beside document_type, so low-confidence 'invoice' labels can be checked by a person
Add an 'other' value plus a document_type_detail string, so unlisted types are captured rather than forced
Add pro_forma and delivery_note to the enum, which covers the two types that have been mislabelled so far
questions.explain: An enum with no escape value forces every unlisted document into the closest listed type. An 'other' value with a detail field captures them honestly. Adding the two types is the near-miss: it fixes today's cases, but the next unlisted type will be forced into an existing label in the same way. Free text loses the downstream routing the enum provides, and a confidence field doesn't stop the forced label.

questions.q: Two outputs: short tag lists shown to people on a dashboard, where a rare format slip is harmless, and invoice records posted to an ERP that rejects anything off-schema. Which pairing matches method to strictness?
options: Prompt-based formatting for the dashboard tags; a prefilled opening brace for the ERP invoice records
Prompt-based formatting for both, with a retry whenever a response fails to parse on the way through
Prompt-based formatting for the dashboard tags; tool use with a JSON schema, forced, for the ERP records
Tool use with a JSON schema for the dashboard tags; a prefilled opening brace for the ERP invoice records
questions.explain: Pick the method by how strict the output must be. A loose, human-read output can use prompt-based formatting, while a system that rejects anything off-schema needs tool use with a schema and the tool forced. The prefill for the ERP is the near-miss: it makes the reply start as JSON, but nothing makes the rest match the schema (and prefill is not supported on the newest models anyway). Parse-and-retry accepts failures as routine, and the last option puts the strict method on the output that needs it least.

questions.q: The pipeline has extract_invoice, extract_receipt and extract_contract tools. Each document must go through exactly one of them, chosen by the model from the content. Which tool_choice setting fits?
options: auto, letting the model decide whether to call one of the tools or answer with text about the document
A forced tool naming extract_invoice, since invoices are most common and the others can be retried
any, which requires the model to call one of the tools while leaving it free to choose the right one
none, followed by a second request asking the model which of the three tools it would use instead
questions.explain: any guarantees a tool call while letting the model pick which one fits the document. auto is the near-miss: the model will usually pick a tool, but auto allows a plain-text reply, which breaks the pipeline's guarantee. Forcing extract_invoice sends receipts and contracts through the wrong schema, and none just adds a round trip.

questions.q: An invoice's line items add up to 1,180.00 but its stated total is 1,250.00. The schema has both stated_total and calculated_total. How should the extraction handle the mismatch?
options: Set stated_total to 1,180.00, since the line items are more detailed and the printed total is likely a typo
Retry the extraction until the two values agree, since a mismatch means the model misread one of them
Record both values as found and flag the mismatch, so the document is routed for review rather than fixed
Keep only stated_total, since it is the figure printed on the document and the one the vendor will bill
questions.explain: Extracting the stated and calculated totals separately exists to surface discrepancies like this one, for a person to resolve. Retrying until they agree is the near-miss: retries help when the model misread something, but here the document itself is inconsistent, so retries either loop or push the model to alter a value to force agreement. Overwriting the stated total destroys evidence, and dropping the calculated total hides the problem.

questions.q: Validation-retry fixes a date returned as '13/04/2025' instead of ISO, but loops until the retry cap when vat_number fails validation on one region's invoices. Most of those invoices carry no VAT number. What is the right change?
options: Allow vat_number to be null when it's absent, and keep retry-with-feedback for errors the document can fix
Raise the retry cap for vat_number, since some regions need more attempts before the model finds the value
Send the validator's error text back on each retry, so the model learns exactly what format the field expects
Turn off vat_number validation for that region, accepting whatever value the model returns for those invoices
questions.explain: Retrying with feedback fixes format and reading errors, but it can't produce information the document doesn't contain. Absent values need a valid null. Sending the error text back is the near-miss: it is the right technique for the date problem, but no feedback can make a missing VAT number appear, and pressure to pass validation invites fabrication. A higher cap means more loops, and turning off validation lets bad values through.

questions.q: Extraction uses a strict JSON schema (strict: true) enforced through tool use. Which TWO kinds of error can still get through? (Select 2)
options: Line items whose amounts don't add up to the stated total
The buyer's name placed in the vendor_name field by mistake
A required field missing from the object the model returns
A number field holding text such as 'twelve hundred' instead
questions.explain: Strict schema enforcement guarantees structure, meaning required fields are present and types are correct, but it can't check meaning. Totals that don't add up and a value placed in the wrong field are semantic errors that need separate validation. The type error is the tempting pick because it feels like a content mistake, but a string in a number field is exactly what a strict schema rejects.

questions.q: Extraction is accurate on clean typed invoices but inconsistent on invoices with handwritten corrections, sometimes taking the struck-out amount. How should you use few-shot examples to fix this?
options: Add 20 examples of clean typed invoices covering varied layouts and correctly extracted totals
Add 2-4 examples of corrected invoices showing which amount to take and why the other is wrong
Add one handwritten example and tell the model to copy its extracted values for any similar documents
Remove all examples, so the model reasons from the schema alone instead of copying example patterns
questions.explain: A few targeted examples of the hard case, with the reasoning shown (ideally including an ambiguous case), teach the model how to resolve that kind of ambiguity. Twenty clean examples is the near-miss: it adds few-shot volume, but all of it is the case the model already gets right, and none shows how to handle a correction. Copying one example's values invites fabrication, and removing examples throws away the most effective lever.

questions.q: All five few-shot examples come from one vendor whose invoices label the total 'Amount Due'. On other vendors' invoices labelled 'Balance' or 'Total Payable', the model often returns null. What is the best fix?
options: Add an instruction listing every total label seen so far, so the model can match each one of them exactly
Add five more examples from the same vendor, so the model gets a stronger signal of what a total looks like
Make total a required field, so the model can't return null and has to find a value on every invoice
Replace some examples with invoices from other vendors and layouts, so the set shows varied total labels
questions.explain: The examples taught one template too well. Varied examples show the model that the concept, the amount payable, matters more than any particular label. The label list is the near-miss: it fixes the labels already seen, but the model learns to match strings rather than understand the field, so the next new label fails. More examples from the same vendor deepen the over-fit, and making the field required forces fabrication.

questions.q: A new client starts sending scanned customs declarations, a type the pipeline has never processed. Accuracy on existing types is 98%, and the team proposes auto-approving the new type like the others. What should happen first?
options: Auto-approve them but route fields with low confidence scores to review, as the pipeline does for other types
Auto-approve them, since 98% across existing types shows the pipeline generalises well to new documents
Add two customs declarations as few-shot examples, then auto-approve the new type from the next batch on
Measure accuracy on a labelled sample of customs declarations, keeping them in human review until it holds up
questions.explain: Automation has to be validated per document type, and a type the pipeline has never seen has no accuracy record yet. Routing by confidence is the near-miss: it is the right routing design once confidence is calibrated, but the scores have never been checked against labelled customs declarations, so they can't yet be trusted to catch errors. Accuracy on other types says nothing about this one, and adding examples is not measuring.

questions.q: Reviewers can check about 10% of extracted documents. Today that 10% is picked uniformly at random, and most of what they see is clean. Which TWO belong in a better review design? (Select 2)
options: Keep picking the reviewed 10% uniformly at random across all types
Send documents with low calibrated field-level confidence to review
Send the longest 10% of documents to review, as they are the hardest
Audit a stratified random sample of auto-approved docs by doc type
questions.explain: Routing by calibrated field-level confidence puts reviewer time where errors are likely, and a stratified sample of auto-approved documents keeps measuring accuracy for each type, so silent failures show up. Uniform random routing is the tempting pick because it gives unbiased accuracy figures, but as the main way to choose what gets reviewed it wastes most of the capacity on clean documents. Length is a weak proxy for difficulty.

questions.q: A bank statement extraction scored 0.95 document-level confidence, yet its IBAN field was wrong. Which design catches errors like this?
options: A higher document-level threshold of 0.99, so only near-certain extractions skip the human review queue
Field-level confidence scores, calibrated against labelled data, with low-scoring fields sent for review
Asking the model to double-check its own output and restate its overall confidence after a second look
Rejecting any document whose overall confidence falls below the team's average for that document type
questions.explain: One document-level score averages over fields, so a single critical wrong field can hide behind a high score. Calibrated field-level confidence exposes it. The 0.99 threshold is the near-miss: it tightens the gate, but it is still one number for the whole document, so a confident document with one bad IBAN still passes. Self-checking in the same context and comparing with an average have the same blind spot.

questions.q: In an agentic loop built on the Messages API, which response tells your code to run the requested tools and call the model again?
options: stop_reason is 'tool_use': the response contains tool calls that need results before the model can continue
stop_reason is 'end_turn': the model has finished its turn and is now waiting for the tools to be executed
stop_reason is 'max_tokens': the model ran out of room and needs the tool output to finish its answer
stop_reason is 'stop_sequence': the model hit a marker separating its text from the tool calls it made
questions.explain: tool_use means the response contains tool_use blocks: run them, append the results, and call again. end_turn is the near-miss: it is the other value the loop checks, but it means the model is done, so the loop should exit. max_tokens means the output was cut off, and stop_sequence means a custom stop string was hit. Neither asks for tool results.

questions.q: A coordinator has two AgentDefinitions and keeps sending database questions to the docs-writer subagent instead of the sql-analyst. Which field most directly governs that choice?
options: prompt, the subagent's system prompt, which tells it what role to play once the coordinator invokes it
description, which tells the coordinator what the subagent is for and when it should be delegated to
tools, the list of tools the subagent may use, which the coordinator inspects to judge what each can do
model, which sets the model the subagent runs on and signals which one handles the harder questions
questions.explain: The coordinator picks a subagent from its description, so vague or overlapping descriptions send work to the wrong one. prompt is the near-miss: it shapes how the subagent behaves once chosen, but the coordinator doesn't read it when deciding who to delegate to. The tools list limits what the subagent can do, and model sets which model runs it. Neither guides the routing.

questions.q: An agent must never call delete_record on production tables, without exception. Which mechanism gives a deterministic guarantee?
options: A system-prompt rule stating the restriction in capital letters, repeated again at the end of the prompt
A few-shot example showing the agent refusing a production delete and explaining the policy to the user
A PostToolUse hook that logs every delete_record call, so violations can be reviewed and rolled back
A PreToolUse hook that inspects delete_record calls and blocks any that target a production table
questions.explain: Only code that runs before the tool executes can guarantee a call never happens, and a PreToolUse hook can deny it outright. The PostToolUse hook is the near-miss: it is also a hook, which makes it look deterministic, but it runs after the delete, so it can only report the damage. Prompt rules and few-shot examples improve the odds but guarantee nothing.

questions.q: You named a Claude Code session 'payments-audit' last week and want to continue it today, though you have run other sessions since. Which command does that?
options: claude --continue, which reopens the session you most recently named in this working directory
claude --fork-session payments-audit, which reopens that session and keeps adding to its history
claude -p payments-audit, which loads that session non-interactively and prints where it left off
claude --resume payments-audit, which reopens that named session with its full history in place
questions.explain: --resume with a session name or id reopens that exact session. --continue is the near-miss: it does resume, but it picks the most recent conversation in the directory, which after other sessions isn't this one. --fork-session goes with --resume to branch into a new session rather than continue the original, and -p treats its argument as a prompt.

questions.q: A single agent has 18 tools covering search, billing, scheduling and reporting, and it increasingly picks the wrong one. What is the most effective change?
options: Give the agent a longer system prompt explaining when to use each of the 18 tools, with an example of each
Set tool_choice to any, so the agent must call a tool on every turn and can't skip the selection step
Split the work across specialised subagents, each holding only the four or five tools its role requires
Rename the tools with category prefixes such as billing_ and search_, so the model can group them by name
questions.explain: Tool selection gets worse as the number of tools grows. Giving each specialised agent a small, role-specific set fixes the cause. Category prefixes are the near-miss: they make the list easier to scan, but the agent still chooses from 18 tools. A longer prompt adds context without reducing the choice, and any forces a call without improving which one.

questions.q: An agent's system prompt says 'Always check the knowledge base first.' The agent now calls search_kb before every action, even for order-status questions that lookup_order answers directly. What is happening?
options: The prompt's wording steers tool choice toward search_kb; reword it to say when the knowledge base applies
search_kb's description is too short, so the model can't tell when it applies and calls it by default
lookup_order is listed after search_kb, and the model tries tools in the order they appear in the request
The model needs tool_choice forced to lookup_order for order questions, since it can't route them itself
questions.explain: Keywords and absolute wording in the system prompt strongly shape tool selection, so 'always check the knowledge base' becomes a rule to call search_kb every time. The short description is the near-miss: thin descriptions do cause misrouting, but here the behaviour follows the prompt's 'always', not uncertainty about the tool. Tool order doesn't set priority, and forcing tool_choice per question type is unnecessary once the wording is fixed.

questions.q: How should an MCP tool tell the model that a call failed, so the model reacts to the failure rather than treating it as data?
options: Return an empty result, so the model notices there is no data and infers that the call must have failed
Throw an exception in the server, so the client ends the session and reports the error to the user directly
Return the error text as a normal result, since the model reads every result and will spot the error message
Return the result with isError set to true and a message saying what went wrong and whether to retry
questions.explain: isError marks the result as a failure, and a clear message lets the model decide whether to retry, adjust or report it. Returning the error text as a normal result is the near-miss: the model may notice it, but nothing marks it as a failure, so it can be taken as real output. An empty result looks like a successful search that found nothing, and crashing the session removes any chance to recover.

questions.q: An MCP tool returns structured errors that include isRetryable. Which TWO failures should be marked retryable? (Select 2)
options: The upstream API timed out before returning any response
The caller lacks permission to read the requested record
The upstream API returned 429 Too Many Requests for the call
The date argument failed validation: '2025-13-40' is invalid
questions.explain: Timeouts and rate limits are transient, so the same call may succeed later. Permission and validation failures will fail again until something changes. The validation error is the tempting pick because the agent can fix it and try again, but that is a corrected new call, not a retry of the same one, so it is not marked retryable. A permission failure needs a different caller or a human.

questions.q: Your team needs Claude to work with GitHub issues and pull requests, and a maintained GitHub MCP server already exists. What is the recommended starting point?
options: Build a custom MCP server, so the tool names and descriptions match the team's own GitHub workflow exactly
Skip MCP and have Claude call the GitHub REST API through Bash and curl, with a token in the environment
Wrap the GitHub CLI in a custom MCP server, so the team controls every command the agent is able to run
Use the maintained GitHub MCP server, and build custom tools only for needs it doesn't already cover
questions.explain: Prefer an existing, maintained server over building your own, and add custom tools only for the gaps. Wrapping the GitHub CLI is the near-miss: it feels like a light, controlled build, but it is still a custom server to maintain, duplicating one that already exists. A fully custom server costs even more, and raw curl through Bash gives up structured tool definitions.

questions.q: Your review findings schema has file, line, severity and message. You want to find which rules cause most false positives so you can tune the criteria. Which added field helps most?
options: A confidence field holding the model's self-rated certainty, so low-certainty findings can be filtered
A detected_pattern field naming the rule or code pattern that triggered each finding, for analysis
A reasoning field holding the model's full explanation, so developers can read why it flagged the code
A timestamp field recording when each finding was made, so you can follow trends in volume over time
questions.explain: detected_pattern tags each finding with what triggered it, so dismissed findings can be grouped by pattern and the noisy criteria found and rewritten. The confidence field is the near-miss: it helps filter findings, but it doesn't tell you which rule produced a false positive, which is what you need in order to tune the criteria. Free-text reasoning is hard to group, and timestamps show volume, not cause.
